How to Think About Knowledge

Building a knowledge system is less about the tools you use and more about the habits you build around capturing, refining, and revisiting ideas. The notes that survive long enough to compound into understanding tend to share a few common properties, which we will explore in the sections below.

Section One

The most important habit is writing in your own words. A literal quote is not yet an evergreen note. It only becomes one when you reformulate the idea in language that fits your own mental model, then connect it to other notes you already trust.

Each evergreen note should make a single claim and stand on its own. If a note depends on context from somewhere else to be understood, that dependency is friction that compounds every time you revisit the idea.

Section Two

The second habit is link density. A note with no outgoing links is a dead end; a note with many links becomes a hub that lets your future self navigate the structure of your own thinking. Links should feel earned, never decorative.

Over time, the graph these links form will start to surface patterns you did not consciously plan for. That emergence is the real payoff of treating your notes as a long-lived knowledge system instead of a collection of disposable scratch files.
